1.	Has the Government received a copy of a resolution adopted by the Legislature of British Columbia on December 1, 1921, (which sets out that at a conference between the federal Government and the Government of British [DOT]Columbia, the federal Government accepted responsibility for the initiation and administration of legislation relating to Mother's Pensions, Old age Pensions and other problems relating to the Improvement of Social Conditions?
2.	If so, what were the terms of such agreement as aforesaid?
3.	Will legislation be introduced this session to give effect to it and to establish Old Age Pensions in Canada?

1. A copy of a resolution of the Legislative Assembly of British Columbia, passed on December 2 last, was received by the federal government on December 12. This resolution refers to a conference which was alleged to have been held between representatives of the Dominion government and provincial governments at Ottawa in 1919. It is stated that consideration was given on this occasion to the responsibilities of the Dominion and provincial administrations with regard to the initiation and administration of legislation relative to mothers' pensions, old age pensions, and other problems relating to the improvement of social conditions, and that it was the understanding of the representatives of British Columbia at this meeting that the Dominion government accepted full responsibility for the enactment of legislation dealing with old age pensions. The resolution of the Legislative Assembly endorsed the principle of old age pensions and directed the attention of the federal authorities to the desirabiltiy of legislation being enacted.
A resolution was adopted unanimously at the National Industrial Conference, which was held in 1919, of Dominion and provincial representatives with representative employers and labour men in favour of the appointment of a board or boards to inquire into the subjects of state insurance against unemployment, sickness, invalidity and old age. The text of this resolution appears in the published report of the National Industrial Conference. The published report, however, contains no reference to any separate conference between the Dominion and provincial ministers on the subjects referred to in the resolution of the Legislative Assembly of British Columbia, and there is nothing on record in the Privy Council office on the subject. Presumably, therefore, any discussions which may have occurred between the federal and provincial ministers on these matters were of an informal nature.
2 and 3. Answered by No. 1.

Occupational Diseases

Mr. HERMAS DESLAURIERS (St. Mary, Montreal) (Translation) moved the following proposed resolution:
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the fact that an act already exists for the protection of workmen agaiinst accidents while engaged in their work, it is desirable that same protection be afforded to all workmen contracting sickness while performing, or due to performance of their work or trade, inasmuch as the federal Government is concerned.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there exists in Canada and in almost every civilized country laws which are so framed as to safeguard the workman against accidents resulting while fulfilling his duties in the various occupations, such as: in house building, mills, factories, ship-yards, shipbuilding, loading and unloading of vessels, public stores, mines, quarries and in all establishments where explosives are manufactured; in all places where machinery driven by any kind -of motor is utilized; these laws entitle the victims or their representatives to an indemnity the nature and importance of which are determined, I believe that in the case of a person disabled or where death is caused by diseases said to be occupational, this person should derive some benefit if not from the Insurance Act against accidents at least from similar legislation. This legislation would apply not to all diseases in general, but to special diseases pertaining to certain industries which are responsible sometimes for the death of those who are so employed. They are also the cause of frequent unemployment the character of which is well known and are thus well termed occupational diseases. At the opening of the Congress for Labour legislation on accidents held at Berne, Switzerland, in 1891, Mr. Numa Droz thus expressed himself: " It is evident that the question of accidents is intimately interwoven with other labour questions. The one dealing with accidents to workmen, if we justly include, within its scope, occupational diseases forms as it were the centre and heart of labour legislation."
In the meantime, the views of Mr. Numa Droz have been embodied in the laws of Switzerland and occupational diseases are included in the liabilities to which industries are subject; this gives rise to claims whether mere unemployment or death be the outcome, and compensation is adequately determined in each case. The word accident is very broad in its acceptation; very

much so, when it stands as an equivalent for disability; wounds resulting from or in connection with the work of the labourer. An accident may be defined: the act by which the human body or parts thereof are affected or destroyed under the influence of unforeseen events. The human body or any part of it, through the medium of some morbid agent may be the cause of disability or of death, whether instantaneous or otherwise.
However, in all cases the employer should be held responsible towards the victim of the accident. Any morbid cause, whatever may be the name given to this agent, let it be called belt, pulley, dynamo, elevator, phosphorous, copper, lead, quicksilver, etc., the name is nothing-any morbid cause which produces disability or death at any period, by impairing or destroying the human body, in my opinion, should give rise to damages whether it is followed by ordinary unemployment, or death be the consequence. Take for instance a labourer who receives a -wound or fractures one of his limbs while working, if as a consequence tetanus or mortification sets in and causes death, certainly the employer is held responsible. Let the end come after five days or months, that does not prevent the claim to be well founded, because one part or a number of parts of the human body have been impaired and then destroyed, within a certain time, creating disability or death through a morbid process which is brought on by the wound at first, and then followed by complications throughout the whole system.
Let us now consider certain cases of occupational diseases, the existence of which is well known. Persons who are employed in the manufacture of chemical matches or in pyrotechnical works-and they are numerous-are subject, owing to the nature of the work, to different accidents. Sometimes the matter which enters into the preparation of matches ignites and explodes and is often the cause of burns; in such cases there can be no doubt that the manufacturer, as proprietor, is to be held responsible. Accompanying the dangers in the nature of accidents, which may result from certain manipulations, to workmen engaged in the manufacture of chemical matches, there exists another more serious danger. It is a disease which has been called by the workmen themselves phosphorous poisoning and which science designates as "necrosis." It consists in the mortification of the facial and jaw bones

Occupational Diseases
leading to disability and very often causing death. This disease is not general amongst the workmen; it affects but a few, and that is precisely why we may say that these persons have been victims of an accident which pertains to the special danger of the occupation followed, the work they are called upon to perform. This disease is the result of the phosphorous fumes which escape from ordinary phosphorous- the only one to which these accidents are attributed, as the c^se is not so with amorphous phosphorous or other substances. The use of the ordinary phosphorous in match factories was prohibited by the French government in 1889, thanks to the efforts of Dr. David and Mr. Truillot, because it was proved that the use of this process developed necrosis. Later, not having been able to enforce this decree, all possible precautions were taken to minimize this danger, the nature of the disease being well defined as occupational, owing to the substance that the workman is obliged to handle and the fumes which he inhales. [DOT]
Upon the advice of Dr. Brouardel and the public health committee, the legislation had to be amended so as to oblige match manufacturers to have their employees examined every month instead of every six months. It is evident that this precaution of compelling the workmen to undergo a strict monthly inspection, in order to find out whether, during this short interval, they have not contracted a disease which is not generally contracted elsewhere, is proof that this disease is more especially an occupational one. Therefore, it would only be fail as well as necessary, to give the workman who is constantly exposed to this danger which he cannot escape, the benefit of the legislation which is his protection in case of an accident when he is at work. After having examined the workman, the medical attendant of the factory, according to his diagnosis of the case, either prescribes a rest, or giving up of the work, should he deem it necessary. The first prescription is usually the extraction of the teeth, a surgical operation required by the disease. But, that to which I shall particularly call your attention, and that which is of the greatest concern to me, is the fact that the workman is compelled to cease all work, and that this unemployment in which he, himself, has nothing to say, is enforced upon him by the medical attendant. This unemployment system had been in practice in France, until Mr. Faure and
several of his colleagues obtained that the workman who is thus condemned to inactivity should, during the time of unemployment, be treated as if he had been the victim of an accident, while at work, and draw full pay at the match factory.
In 1888, Mr. Felix Faure, admitted the necessity of protecting workmen from these so-called occupational diseases, in reply to Mr. Gabriel Raspail's proposal for such a measure. He told him that his request was quite fair, but that this legislation concerned the health department more than the labour department. Now that we have here, in Ottawa, a health department as well as a labour department, could they not emulate Switzerland and France in this matter of occupational diseases? Although these occupational diseases pertain to health, I think they should be dealt with by the Labour department. As in the case of accidents while on duty, it is a question of indemnifying the workman as much as possible for the injuries caused either by the machinery he uses, or by the material he handles.
The glass industry, where the workman exercises his trade at a temperature frequently of 400 degrees, which suggested the nick name of "fire food," unquestionably breeds an occupational disease. How many times is not the worker, under such an intense fire, overwhelmed by a cerebral congestion that brings on death or apoplexy, leaving paralysis in its wake? What a number of unfortunates come to our offices covered with cutaneous eruptions, as a result of alterations which take place in the blood through inhaling the fumes of ilium inating gas which abounds in those work shops? How many of us have met such persons suffering from enormous distension of the cheeks, often more than an inch beyond the lower jaw-bone, caused by the continuous strain of glass-blowing which makes them say that they have "broken cheeks"-and the same may be said of their lungs. Since statistics show that 26 to 100 of such workmen suffer from cataracts, when forty years old, owing to the intense heat they constantly endure, and since it is known that in those industries, designedly to save coal, steam is forced over the fires, thus subjecting the workman to gaseous and sulphuric emanations that poison them; and that being so, is it possible to deny the occupational character of such diseases?
One of the most widely spread industries in all countries, and one which is the most disastrous because of the occupational dis-
Occupational Diseases

ease it develops, is the textile industry. A staff of employees is imprisoned in buildings the ventilation of which is absolutely deficient; the atmosphere, in the carding and combing rooms, is filled with cotton or flax dust which the men and women breathe constantly, filling their lungs with this in-salubiious dust. This industry requires a humid atmosphere frequently overheated to 35 degrees as in woollen factories. Workers of either sex labour the whole day in an atmosphere laden with steam; they wear damp clothing; their feet are constantly wet: they are obliged to leave the factory in all kinds of weather, be it autumn or winter, at meal time, and when the day's work is over, so that, in a country like ours they are exposed to the most dangerous chills. The class of people who work in these factories is very poor because they receive only famine wages which is not sufficient to provide them with proper shelter, clothing and food; and therefore, the inroads of tuberculosis are far-reaching amongst these people.
If we look into the statistical data concerning textile industries it will be seen that 25 per cent of the people working in those factories fall a prey to tuberculosis.
Among rubber workers, how many cases are there of individuals inhaling carbon sulphide the effects of which upon the brain are such that it may bring on temporary and sometimes permanent insanity, always causing a marked deterioration of the nervous system! In the process of vulcanization, chloride of sulphur injures the respiratory organs, sometimes causing asphyxiation, with the most serious after effects.
It will be sufficient to remember the pitiful experience of our soldiers, the victims of asphyxiating gases on the battlefields, to have a notion of its effects upon the body of a mechanic working in a shop where rubber is vulcanized.
Grinders, 'arm-tool or metal-polishers, using emery, grit or silicate grind-stones, glass-cutters, inhale copper dusts which, combining with the acids in the human body, generate copper sulphate, a very active poison. Emery or silicate dusts emitted by the wheels settle in the lungs of these workingmen and destroy the lung substance to such an extent that a member of the French Assembly, Dr. Armand Des-pres once stated upon the floor of the House that a young man entering those workshops when fifteen years old was carried away by consumption at the age of thirty, and that 
statistical data revealed that eight out of ten were in that predicament.
I could cite many more instances which go to prove that there are occupational diseases which cause disability and even death; those I have already given are sufficient, I think, to support my contention. The law of nature is there to forbid any attempt against the lives of our fellow-men, be it for gain or other reasons, by imposing such conditions of existence or labour as I have mentioned. Money considerations do not entitle us to render a fellow-creature blind or to poison him, so as to accumulate wealth at the expense of his health.
Why should we not be as solicitous for an employee as the owner is for his horse which is hurt or falls sick while at work. Is it not true that in addition to his personal attendance, he gives his horse medicine and a more copious feeding and calls a veterinary surgeon? How different with man! When a working man who has but his day's wages for a living is a prey to sickness as a result of labour conditions, his employer deserts him; his salary is cut off; he gets neither a physician nor medicine and is very often driven to poverty, even if he does not lose his employment. And when sickness is due to the character of his work, should we not be at liberty to say that this man is entitled to some consideration for himself, and his family? In my opinion this is an anomaly and it is the duty of every representative of an industrial constituency to try and suppress such an anomaly, lest later on his parliamentary record be invoked against him and he be charged with selfishness and indifference to the welfare of his constituents.
What a contrast, if we think it over, between this apparent indifference and those national outbursts of sentiment and philanthropy over infant mortality-which I deplore myself. Far-seeing citizens, including women, are sounding the alarm year in and year out; the subject is commented upon from the pulpit and this national calamity is deplored; the medical profession furnishes its quota of apostles; the dispensaries are increasing in number as are literary writings, associations and good advices from lecturers and sacrifices intended to check this scourge. All that,
I admit, is worthy of such a cause; but after all, such admirable zeal is displayed only in order to face unfortunate consequences, it has to be acknowledged, arising from numerous causes the chief of which

Occupational Diseases
are atavism, heredity, want and poverty. Let us begin by safeguarding the maid who toils in our workshops and may be a mother tomorrow; let us protect the man while at his work, especially the father of a family to enable him to bring home regularly, comfort and the necessaries of life, instead of giving to the community young women who are a prey to anaemia, sickness and exhaustion through working in spinning mills, laundries and rubber factories, and instead of marrying them to men intoxicated, poisoned, who bring to their families insufficient wages on account of frequent unemployment. And then the problem of infant mortality will be solved.
What! the laws would not have a single enactment acknowledging the claims of a working man who would come to you and say: I entered the workshop in perfect health; I was not a prey to any ailment and I had not a trace of the disease which afflicts me to-day and which, out of fifty or sixty patients, according to the testimony of medical men, claims twenty and more victims. When a working man will come to you and say: I entered this factory and after four or five years, I began to feel the effects of the disease which has reduced me to unemployment," or when the children in turn will reproach you: "You are responsible for our father's premature death; medical science recognizes and statistics testify that the nature of his work was the cause of his death"; when they will claim damages, will it not be difficult to ignore that this workman was the victim of a truly occupational disease?
I do not quite see the difference between the risks that a workman may incur in a factory, owing to the material he handles exploding or otherwise by poisoning resulting from the same material either by the fumes emitted and inhaled or through any other process of absorption which in a short while may cause disability or death.
What was the object of bringing down a Compensation Act on accidents? The legislator desired $o come to the rescue of the workman, he wished to protect him against his own negligence, and carelessness. He did not take into account if the employer had used poor judgment or was guilty of negligence; he required but one condition for the enforcing of the law. He established the principle, and I think no exception should be made, that where there existed a danger pertaining to the nature of the work itself, thereby occasioning such conditions where accidents take
place and which generally are followed by disability to carry on the work, it was the owner of this industry who should compensate him for the damage caused.
Starting from that established principle which is well recognized in Canada, we must consequently place occupational diseases on the same footing as accidents. We are indebted to the workingmen who fall victims of an explosion either in a mine or a factory. The same indebtedness is due, based on the same principle, to the workingmen who have been victims, in a chemical factory or other, of an occupational disease which has rendered them unfit to work and which sometimes may cause death.
I believe that the two casse are absolutely identical and that it is time to cry out with Waldeck Rosseau, the father of labour syndicates in Prance: "Forward, let us advance, run if necessary, but at least let us make some headway."

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 confess that 1 have not been able to follow all that my hon. friend has said in support of his motion; but in so far as it is his desire to have the federal government Consider the welfare of its employees in matters both cf sickness and of accident, I am in entire sympathy with the purpose that he has in view. I think, however, the motion, as it is worded, goes, beyond this, in that it refers to existing legislation, which is provincial, not federal legislation; and while I should not like to raise the question of the propriety of this House discussing provincial legislation, it is well, I think, to point out the possible bearing of this circumstance before my hon. friend presses his motion to a division. The resolution reads:	[DOT]
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the fact that a law already exists for the protection of workmen against accidents while engaged in their work, it is desirable that same protection be afforded to all workmen contracting sickness.
Workmen's Compensation Acts, as the House well knows, are acts enacted by provincial legislatures, and no doubt provincial legislatures will also consider the question of extending social insurance to include insurance against sickness as well as compensation for accident. But I do not think this House could properly pass upon what the provinces should do in this matter. The resolution, however, is clearly ambiguous. The last clause of all-"inasmuch as the federal government is concerned"

Schooner Con Rein

would seem to indicate that what my hon. friend has in mind is solely the employees of the federal government. As I have already said, as regards the employees of the Government, we may very properly consider whether they should not be protected in the performance of their duties against sickness just as well as against accident, and to that extent, I am wholly in sympathy with my hon. friend's motion. But so far as it involves any expression of opinion as to what should be done by provincial legislatures, I do not think this House should consider the question further. I think my hon. friend's purpose has been well served by the able speech he has made upon the resolution, and by having presented arguments which we can all read when we have an opportunity of perusing the report of the debate.
Do I understand that the hon. member (Mr. Deslauriers) wishes to withdraw his motion?

Yes.
Motion withdrawn.

That in the opinion of this House, immediate steps should he taken hy the Government to restore the pension rights and status of all employees and ex-employees of the Grand Trunk railway who were deprived thereof owing to participation in a strike on the system in the year 1910, to the end that all such may secure their just rights pursuant to the terms and true intent of the settlement made between the parties.
He said: In my absence on April 10, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), referring to this resolution, said:
There is no need for this resolution inasmuch as the Government has already taken steps in the direction proposed. The Government has been negotiating with a view of seeing that a long standing injustice should toe remedied without further delay: If it is not possible to effect by negotiation what we hope and believe will be attained by negotiation, then the Government will bring in the necessary legislation to see that the injustice that was done to employees of the Grand Trunk railway involved in the strike of 1910, in virtue of the terms and conditions of its settlement not having been complied with, is duly remedied.
I read with great interest and satisfaction the remarks of the Prime Minister, and in view of what he said on that occasion I certainly have no desire at the present time to press this motion. I should be glad, however, if my hon. friend

could see his way clear to give me an opportunity later on in the session, if perchance negotiations fail, or if no legislation is brought forward, to deal with the subject matter of this motion. I am very much in earnest about it, and I realize that the Government are as well. Apparently we are in accord in our views, and if the Prime Minister would be kind enough to promise me this consideration I should appreciate it very much and, on the strength of such an assurance, I would move the adjournment of the debate on the motion.

Last year, on the 29th of August, a vessel belonging to the Port of LaHave, in the province of Nova Scotia, was sunk near Block island in the state of Rhode Island, by an American submarine. The circumstances surrounding the collision were investigated by the United States mafine authorities, and in a report which was submitted by that body it was found that Lieutenant John H. Hames, of the United States navy, commanding officer of the United States submarine K-4, was responsible for the collision between that submarine and the three-masted schooner Con Rein. I am instructed that under the conditions that exist in the United States it was not and is not possible for the owners of the ves-

Schooner Con Rein
sel to assert in the law courts, directly as against the United States government, a claim for damages which accrued to them as a result of the sinking of the vessel. Consequently they have petitioned the hon. the Prime Minister as Secretary of State for External Affairs to request the United States government to provide compensation for the loss which they sustained. That petition has come in the ordinary course and, I have no doubt, has been presented to the United States government. I am not aware of the result.
Now, the facts of this matter are so clear that there does not seem to be any doubt about the liability for the collision, and I would ask the Government to use every effort to urge upon the United States government the immediate settlement of the claim. But this affair illustrates the anomalous position of Canada with reference to matters in which Canadian citizens in the United States are interested. In order that any action might be taken in this matter, it is the duty of the Government of Canada to approach the United States government through the British Ambassador at Washington. It does seem to me that there ought to be a more direct method by which the Canadian people could have their interests protected in the American republic than through the diplomatic means now at our disposal through the British Embassy. I am aware that in previous sessions of this Parliament, when I had not the honour to be present, the question of representation at Washington was discussed, and I understand that it was announced as the policy of the late government to appoint a representative at Washington. So far no one has been appointed to such a position. I would submit to this House that many important matters that are continually arising as between the United States and Canada, adjacent as they are to one another, in which the interests of Canadian citizens are involved, require special care and attention; and it is in the interests of this country that a Canadian representative should be appointed to be resident at Washington. Looking over the proceedings of the last Imperial Conference, I gathered that the position of the British government in regard to the matter was that they had no objection to the appointment of such an official, working, of course, in conjunction with and under the British Ambassador. When one comes to think of the tremendous effect on this country of the numerous tariff changes which are made from time to time, and the
legislation of every character passed by the United States Congress, and of the thousand and one other ways which one on a few moments' reflection can call to mind, in which action on the part of the United States government is of considerable interest to the people of Canada, one is forced to the conclusion that we should have a Canadian representative at Washington.
This case illustrates the peculiarly anomalous position in which a Canadian citizen is placed. A vessel has been sunk through the negligence of a United States naval officer, but the owners cannot proceed directly against the government of the United States in the courts of that country, and when they seek the services of our Secretary of State for External Affairs they find that instead of dealing directly with the United States Government, our Secretary of State must approach that government through the British Embassy. Naturally the British Embassy is occupied with very many problems affecting the two countries, and with the delay which is always characteristic of the interchange of communications between governments, a matter such as this is very likely to be pigeon-holed; whereas if we had a Canadian representative in Washington he could take it up immediately with the appropriate department of State there and secure a speedy settlement. All over Canada there must be cases arising in which our citizens are likely to be injuriously affected in the United States, and I submit-although I have not included this proposal in my resolution-that the House might well consider whether we should not hasten the appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington. The injustice which the owners of this vessel have suffered through the inevitable delay in securing a settlement of their claims, and the peculiar position of the whole matter, illustrate to my mind very clearly the necessity of the appointment which I have indicated.

Mr. Speaker, some fifteen years ago I had the honour of accompanying a deputation from Ottawa to attend a gathering at Washington of the North American Lumbermans' Association. We had the honour of being received by the then President of the United States, the late Theodore Roosevelt, and I remember he told us that the intercourse between Canada and the United States was becoming so important that the old roundabout system of dealing between the two countries through
Schooner Con Rein

the Colonial Office was entirely inadequate, and that it demanded that Canada should have nothing less than a representative resident at Washington. The president repeated that statement to several persons in our deputation, and we thanked him for the compliment he was paying to Canada's growing importance. I was of his opinion at that time and I still entertain it. I have had the advantage of hearing the question discussed in this House on many occasions, and it is a wonder to me and to all others who have given it any attention to see, when we go to Washington, insignificant little republics represented there by resident ministers or consul-generals, while this important country, with its many dealings with the United States, is without direct representation. I heartily concur in the view expressed by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and I hope one of the achievements of the government will be to have a permanent representative appointed to Washington so that our relations with our great neighbours will be further advanced as rapidly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to endorse the request of the hon. member for Pictou that action be taken by the Canadian Government in order to get a settlement of the case to which he refers. Although the amount involved is not very large as amounts go to-day, when we are thinking and spending in millions, perhaps the officials of the Government do not realize what the loss means to the people who are directly interested. The company spoken of is doing business in my own county, and is known as the East La Have Transportation Company, Limited. This company owned a vessel named the Con Rein, engaged in the coasting trade between ports in Nova Scotia and New York and other United States ports. At the time the accident happened, last August, the vessel delivered in the port of New York a cargo of lumber and took on board a return cargo of anthracite coal for Charlottetown, P.E.I. On the way down the sound she was rammed by a United States submarine. At the investigation, in which three qualified United States naval officers took part and held court it was conclusively proved that the officers of the submarine were at fault. Not only did the owners lose their ship, which was worth $70,000, but the owner of the cargo was also a loser, and the crew lost all their personal effects.

The owners of the vessel brought the case to the attention of the Canadian Government through their solicitors, and I understand the Department of External Affairs has taken action. But, as large bodies move slowly, not only in Canada but in the United States, I would impress upon the Government the necessity of endeavouring as early as possible to get the United States government to take early action towards a settlement of the owners' claims, and I am sure that after hearing the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou the Government will do their utmost to this end.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Government will be only too pleased to follow up this matter immediately along the lines suggested by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). There is no reason why the motion should not carry.
With regard to the larger question of the direct representation of Canada at Washington, this is receiving the consideration of the Government at the present time.
Motion agreed to.

That, in the opinion of this House, in order to encourage the shipbuilding and fishing industry, it is advisable that every possible assistance be given to the promotion and maintenance of international deep sea racing between Canadian deep sea fishing vessels and deep sea fishing vessels of other nations.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, there are two
questions which I wish to discuss on this resolution-the encouragement that should be given to our shipbuilding industry; and the encouragement that should be given to our fishing industry.
It is a well-known fact, Sir, that shipbuilding has been engaged in since the earliest times of which we have any records. The first vessel that sailed the stormy sea was Noah's ark-and that was a great many years ago. But as you know, Sir, Noah was given inside information of a great flood that was to come, and he was told also to prepare for it and be ready, with his wife and his family, to go into the ark for shelter. That boat, though not, perhaps, as modern a vessel as those we have at the present day, fulfilled the purpose for which it was intended, and, after a number of days passed on the stormy sea, came to rest on mount Ararat.

Deep Sea Racing
Were they fishing?

No, they were not fishing. You will also remember, Sir, from a reading of the history of Greece and Carthagena, that vessels were built in those days not only to sail the seas and carry the products of one nation to the other, but to engage in the fishing industry. Coming down to more modern times, in the sea yarns written by Kingsley, Stevenson and others, we read of the events which took place, especially in the Old Country and the United States, in connection with the building of ships in those days. Before steam came into use, when vessels were entirely propelled by sails, each country vied with the other in an effort to produce ships which would make voyages in the least possible time. We remember that ships sailed from England, went around Cape Horn and the Cape of Good Hope ,and proceeded to India, Australia and New Zealand, or ports on the Pacific coast. They carried goods manufactured in Great Britain, and brought back from India the spices of that land; from China, the teas which were raised there, and from Australia, wool and other products. These stories are very interesting, especially to those who take an interest in the sea. Not only did1 these -ships carry valuable cargoes, but there was vigorous competition between them, prizes being sometimes offered by the owners of vessels to the captains as an inducement to make the shortest possible voyage. There was competition between ships owned by English merchants, and ships owned by Americans. I could go on for a long time, but I do not wish to occupy the attention of the House at too great length in emphasizing the interest taken in the ship-building business in those days, in order that the products of the land -might be carried on the different oceans to far-away countries.
My object this afternoon is to endeavour to show the connection between the building of ships to carry the products of land and sea to foreign countries and a matter of international interest which I think the House should consider. In 1854 a New York pilot boat known as the America was taken across to England to participate in a race in which everybody in the Old Country was interested. In a contest off the I'sle of Wight, at which Queen Victoria was present, the America -defeated the English clipper which sailed against her, and what was known as the International Cup was brought from the Old Country to America. Since that time several attempts have been made to wrest that cup
from the American people and take it back to the British Isles. A number of ships were built for that purpose; Lord Dun-raven, who was a great yachtsman in the Old Country, for -several years competed in this race off New York Harbour, but in all cases the American boat was the better or the faster one, and the cup has ever since remained in the possession of the New York Yacht Club. Sir Thomas Lipton also came across, first with his Shamrock I., and competed against the Vigilant, I think it was. In subsequent years, with the Shamrock II. and Shamrock -III., -he endeavoured without success to wrest that cup from the American yacht club. In my opinion, this competition of -sailing vessels is something which should be encouraged by the people of Canada.
Some four years ago, as the result of a suggestion which I made in a speech at the annual gathering of the Nova Scotia fishermen that a fishing race should be held, some gentlemen in the city of Halifax and others who became interested decided to hold what is known as the fishermen's races. Accordingly, in 1920, off the harbour of Halifax, seven or eight fishing schooners, vessels of 100 tons which had been built for fishing purposes and had actually been engaged in that great industry, took part in a race which was the delight of those who witnessed it. The winner was the Delawana, and some Americans who were present from Gloucester and Boston, and who were interested in the fishing industry and in racing, suggested that there be a contest between the Delawana and a fishing schooner named the Esperanto. I do not need to go into the details of this contest; every man and woman in Canada read of the race which took place off Halifax harbour. One of the Halifax papers donated a challenge cup, known as the International cup, to the winner of this race. The American schooner proved the faster of the two, and she took the cup to the city of Gloucester. Last year the fishing captains and business men of Nova Scotia, with the view of getting the cup back, built several vessels to compete in the race which took place last fall. Several new fishing schooners were built-and I may say that one of the conditions of the race is that vessels taking part in it must have been engaged in fishing during the summer preceding the race. An impetus was thus given to shipbuilding in Nova Scotia as a result of the race in 1920. It will be remembered also that last fall the American fishing schooner Elsie com-

Deep Sea Racing

peted with the schooner Bluenose, built in my own town, for this international cup; and I am pleased to be able to say that the Bluenose, built by one of our enterprising shipbuilding firms, Messrs. Smith and. Ruland, won the race on both days, with the result that the cup came back to Nova Scotia. According to an arrangement arrived at by an international committee composed of men from Nova Scotia, Boston and Gloucester, this year the cup must be defended by a Nova Scotia fishing vessel in Massachusetts Bay. In other words, we have to take our ship over to Massachusetts Bay rather than compete for the cup in home waters. You will have noticed that we have built in Nova Scotia two new schooners to enter the elimination races, with the view of seeing whether they are better than the Bluenose, and that American business men and fishing captains have during the last several months built two vessels to compete in this race. We feel that this is not a local matter; we feel that it is not even a provincial matter, but that it is of interest to the whole people of Canada, because the men who go over to Gloucester will go there as Canadians. Last year when the ship Elsie came down from Gloucester, she did not come alone, but was accompanied by an American naval vessel bringing representatives from many parts of the United States. The President, for instance, sent his own representative; the state of Massachusetts also sent a representative, as did also the city of Boston; the city of Gloucester sent their mayor. When we go this year, I ask the federal government to send their representative, I will also ask the Nova Scotia government to send their representative. So this is not a matter of purely local interest, but one of international interest. It is of interest not only to the province, not only to the whole of this country, but also to the people of the United States as well.
My object in bringing this matter to the attention of the House is this. In view of the fact that this is an international matter, a few people in the province of Nova Scotia, looking at it entirely from a racing and business standpoint, should not be expected to bear the whole cost of this venture. When the race was held in home waters, the cost was not so great and a few gentlemen in Nova Scotia, as I have said, were willing to put up the expenses, but taking part in this race in Massachusetts Bay will mean an extra expense, and while the owners of the Canadian ship are

willing to risk losing their vessel in the race or en route, and also incur the depreciation that is bound to take place in the vessel, whilst she is in the race, they feel that as the country as a whole is interested in this matter, it should contribute something towards the cost. With this race being held year after year, more vessels will be built in the province of Nova Scotia, and more ships will sail on the seas carrying the products of Nova Scotia and of Canada to all parts of the world. It will also be of benefit to the fishing industry, which, in my humble opinion, has not had the encouragement in the past which it should have received. If the Government takes an interest in this matter and grants a small sum of money, I believe that not only will the shipbuilding industry be encouraged and more vessels be built to go on the high seas and the Grand Banks of Newfoundland to bring into the ports of Nova Scotia the products of the sea, but that the fishing industry also will be materially improved. I need not tell you, Mr. Speaker, why this encouragement should be given. The deep sea fishing fleet of Nova Scotia, and after all, that really means the deep sea. fishing fleet of Canada, is a great asset to this country, and the Government would make no mistake in encouraging these hardy toilers of the sea, who go down to the sea in ships and risk their lives day after day on the ocean. It is a beautiful sight,- and if you saw it, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you would agree with me-to see about one hundred and twenty-five schooners, of about one hundred tons, hoisting their flags and making ready for the fishing grounds. They do not hoist the flag every day for the wind to blow it to tatters. The flag to the fishermen of Nova Scotia and their wives and sweethearts is an emblem and a symbol. It is a sacred matter. The fishermen of Nova Scotia do not believe in flapping the flag, they only fly the flag on special occasions. When these vessels are ready for sea their captains go to the custom house and clear for the deep, and the flag is hoisted to the masthead. It is a symbol that the vessel is ready to sail on an adventurous voyage, and that the crew are about to take risks that perhaps no other men in the world have to take in their daily occupation. The men down there do not cheapen the flag by raising it every day. They reserve it for this one special occasion when they clear for the Banks, when it is used as a symbol and an emblem that they are sailing out on the deep waters, to be away perhaps for two or

Deep Sea Racing
three months. Again, when the vessels return and are seen in the offing, perhaps three or four miles away, we go on the hill-tops with our binoculars and see the flag flying at the masthead, and we go down and raise our own flag to show, first that the men on board have safely returned, and secondly to signal that their families have been well while they were away. That is what we fly the flag for. It is a beautiful sight, I say, to see these ships with their flags flying, going out to sea and returning to port.
These men deserve some consideration from this Government. If we can vote $1,000 for Alpine climbers, as we are doing, and for other services not so deserving, I think this Government, in order to encourage the building of ships and the development of the fishing industry in this country might very well make a small grant for this purpose. It is a matter that is of interest to the whole people of Canada. I remember last year when the race was on, we were having inquiries from all over the country as to how it was going, and the telegraph offices kept open all night so that news of the race could be flashed every three minutes. I therefore think that Parliament should have no hesitation in voting the small sum of $5,000 for this very worthy object.
Shipbuilding and the fishing industry is no new thing in Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia all revere the memory of Hon. Joseph Howe, one of the greatest statesmen Canada has ever produced. We remember that when he was in this Parliament he gave expression to the opinion that in forty years from that date we would have at least 500,000 men engaged in the fishing industry in Nova Scotia. These hopes, however, have not been realized, and it seems to me this Liberal Government should endeavour as far as possible to realize the hopes of the great people of Nova Scotia. What did Joseph Howe say about these men? I think perhaps it is worthy of being put on the pages of Hansard:
Though my craft may be small, she is snug and she's trim,
And her crew are accustomed to battle the wave,
They are cheerful of heart, and athletic of limb,
And follow the business their bold fathers
gave.
Through the storm and the sleet of the winter we sail,
While the rich and the feeble on couches repose;
There is health in our toil, and a charm in the
gale,
And our courage still rises the harder it blows.
88i
Every harbor from Sable to Canso's a home,
Every depth from the Banks to St. Lawrence we've tried,
And we care not though round Labrador we may roam,
Or sweep on the strength of old Fundy's fierce tide.
Now wealth from the waves we draw forth with our lines.
And now with a cargo of produce we're stow'd,
Or having a full freight of coal from the mines,
We slowly sail on with our cumbersome load. Then who would exchange the rough life that we lead,
Joint owners at sea, and free sons of the soil, At the bidding of others to labour and bleed
With but little of pleasure to sweeten our toil.
We build our own shallops-
That is what we do in Nova Scotia. It is a joint venture. Nearly every fisherman on board one of these fishing vessels, which cost perhaps $35,000, is an owner in the venture.
We build our own shallops, we rear our own crew,
And life has for us sweet endearment in store, For though luxury's fetters our souls never knew,
Bright eyes bid us welcome when peril is o'er.
I think that is a most beautiful sentiment. I think it covers the whole ground, and that there is no necessity for me to argue further. I might, however, say that the shipbuilding industry in Nova Scotia needs some encouragement. All during the war we built every vessel it was possible for us to build, at the call of our country, but conditions have changed. Freights are now low, and if some encouragement is not given the shipbuilding industry in Nova Scotia, I am afraid there will not be many vessels built in the next few years. Therefore, not only to encourage the shipbuilding industry, but the fishing industry as well, so that we shall have more fishing vessels going down to the sea and bringing back its products for the whole people of this country, I think this Government would be very well advised to accept my motion and include in the supplementary estimates a small grant of $5,000 for this purpose.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) :
speechtext:
I am sure every
member of this House feels grateful to my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) for the information he has given us. His remarks certainly appealed to my sporting and national spirit, when I realized that the Nova Scotia fishermen were holding their own against the Americans and other foreign competitors in the race. I must admit his eloquent words appealed to my
Immigration Act

poetic feeling. If, as my hon. friend says, the encouragement of the Government would help the fishing and shipbuilding industry in that province, certainly some assistance should be given. I do not know whether the enthusiastic expression of my hon. friend "every possible assistance" can be accepted. It is rather wide. I have not given the matter sufficient consideration to commit the Government to any expenditure at the present time, but I promise my hon. friend that I shall give this matter full consideration, and I ask the House to allow me to move the adjournment of the debate so that I may later on convey to my hon. friend the decision of the Government on the question.
