House again in Committee on Bill No. 16-Mr. Woodsworth- to amend the Immigration Act, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: At the time of the second reading of this bill, the Government expressed the view that, perhaps, it had better be considered by a special committee. I understand, having made inquiries from different groups in the House, that some exception has been taken by one of the groups to having the bill go to a special committee, and it was thought more desirable to have it discussed in Committee of the Whole. The Government has no objection to proceeding with the bill in Committee of the Whole, in order to see what progress we will make, and I am inclined to think, from the intricate nature of the bill, that it would be an advantage all round to carry out the original suggestion and send it to a special committee.

The suggestion
of the Prime Minister that the bill should be considered by a smaller committee is quite satisfactory to me, if it meets with the approval of the House. I recognize the difficulty of dealing in a general committee with the complicated question involved. I do not know just what the order of procedure is at this point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The order is to proceed in Committee of the Whole and see how we get along.

In order that we may intelligently discuss the first subsection, it will be necessary to give very briefly an outline as to what is proposed

by this bill. The matter was not discussed on the second reading because it was thought that the bill would go to a smaller committee. The effect of the existing amendment to the Immigration Act is really to deprive a very large section of our people of the right to trial by jury- a very serious consideration. It is unnecessary for me to review the history of the claims put forth by the British people, from the time of the Magna Charta and the Bill of Rights, to the night of trial by jury. That great document-the Magna Charta-was effective in restricting the arbitrary power of kings and ministers, but we have to-day, in this legislation which has been placed on the statute book, a reversion, if I may call it so, to the condition of affairs which prevailed before the time of the Magna Charta. There are three acts which are very intimately connected. The first, is the amendment to the Immigration Act, with an amendment to the amendment, the second is the Naturalization Act, and the third is the amendment to the Criminal Code which was introduced at the same time. Those three acts dovetail into one another and have the effect of taking away the right of trial by jury from a very considerable section of the people of Canada. This act is designed primarily, not, as one might imagine from its being an Immigration Act, to keep out undesirable immigrants, but rather to deal with people who are already in Canada. I submit that, if we are going to deal with undesirable people in Canada, or people who have committed crimes in Canada, the provision with regard to that ought not to be brought in, in connection with an immigration law. Let me repeat. This act is not designed to keep people out of this country, but rather to deal with people who are already here. It may be said; roughly, that there are four classes of people in Canada: First, the native-born, either of English or French or other origin; second, immigrants from the United States, who are technically foreigners, but whom we very largely regard as belonging to the same class of people as we are; third, those whom we commonly class as foreigners, who speak some other language than English as their mother tongue, people who come, very largely, from various countries of Europe; and fourth, British-born people, people who belong to the same stock as we do, but who have been born in England, Scotland, Ireland or other British countries. To-day, as a Canadian-born Britisher, I should like

Immigration Act
to appeal to my fellow Canadian-born Britishers, whether English or French, to relieve the British-born of the disabilities under which they are placed in Canada because of their birth in Great Britain. That is the situation as it exists to-day.
Let me deal now with the various sections of the bill. The first one has to do with domicile, and this can be understood only as we remember that the idea is to get rid of certain undesirable classes. These classes are enumerated in later sections of the act; the first provision makes it impossible for anyone, later classed as an undesirable, to obtain domicile in Canada. These people can come into this country and they may live here for a certain period of time; but if they are declared to be undesirable, it is as if they were not living here; their residence here gives them no claim whatever, no right to trial in the courts of this country. They may have been living quite a harmless life; they may have no criminal record against them, either in the Old Country or in this country; but if they are declared to be undesirable, the fact that they have been living here actually ceases to have any value.
They are declared to be undesirable by the immigration authorities, I understand, not by a court of justice.

Quite so. That
is the point. This is entirely under the Immigration Act, and my plea is that, before anybody, who has been living in this country for any length of time, is declared undesirable, his case should be presented to a regular court and decided by that court, and not by the Immigration Department or any other department. That is why I seek to have this particular section altered. Section 2 of the act provides :
Provided further that no person who belongs to the prohibited or undesirable classes within the meaning of section 41 of this act shall be capable of acquiring Canadian domicile.
Then again, subsection (ii) in part reads:
Canadian domicile is lost, for the purposes
of this act	by any person belonging to
the prohibited or undesirable classes within the meaning of section 41 of this act.
Then again subsection (iii) in part reads:
When any citizen of Canada who is a British subject by naturalisation, or any British subject not born in Canada having Canadian domicile, shall have resided for one year outside of Canada, he shall be presumed to have lost Canadian domicile.
That is, if a man, who has been living in this country for a considerable number of years, should, for instance, return to Great Britain for a year to visit his people and then come back to Canada, he would cease to have Canadian domicile and cease to have any right to trial in this country.
Although a British subject?

Let us be clear on that point. Although a British subject, he would cease to have any rights whatever before the courts of this country. That is the point with regard to the first clause of the Bill. If I may, I would like to run briefly over the other clauses, as they are closely inter-related. I pass on to the second clause repealing paragraphs (n), (o) and (p) of subsection 6 of section-there is a typographical error there; that should be section 3 instead of section 2. The amendment to the act adds a number of classes to those who had previously been regarded as undesirable. The objectionable feature is contained in these words:
Persons . . . . (n) who disbelieve in or are opposed to organised Government. . . . (o) persons who are members of or affiliated with any organisation entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organised Government.
And:
(p) Enemy aliens or persons who have been alien enemies and who were or may be interned on or after the eleventh day of November, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen, in any part of His Majesty's Dominions or by any of His Majesty's allies.
I think it is quite obvious to any one that I am not here to advocate, in any way whatever, disbelief in organized government. But I do say that this question of belief or disbelief in organized government and the decision whether people do or do not believe in this, should not be left to an Immigration Department. That is the point. The question should be left to the courts. This matter ought to be kept very clearly before us as we proceed. I can quite understand how many people may misunderstand the position which I am trying to put forward, because, on the face of the matter, one would say: "Is that not reasonable? Should we not try to exclude people who disbelieve in organized government?" I would be quite willing to say: "Yes." But if people come into this country and are resident in this country, it ought not to be within the power of any individual in the Immigration Department
Immigration Act

or any other department to say: "You are here and since you disbelieve in organized government, you must be sent out of the country without any trial on the matter whatever." Worse than that, this paragraph (p) works a gross injustice to a large number of our fellow citizens who are technically classed as alien enemies. A good many people whom I know in the West, who came from those provinces in Austria, which lie along the border line between Austria and Russia and which were overridden first by one army and then by the other, when the war broke out, were within the bounds of Austria, and hence came to be classed as alien enemies. I protest, incidentally, this was a great injustice to them. As one of those men said to me one day: "We were enemies of Austria long before Great Britain was an enemy of Austria; we came out to this country to get away from Austria." Yet the fact that they had been born in Austria classed them as alien enemies. We find this section dealing with these people who are in this country, many of whom have been living exemplary lives, the very class of people whom perhaps we most need as immigrants to go on the land. The clause reads:
Enemy aliens or persons who have been alien enemies and who were or may be interned on or after November 11, 1918.
So that this is directed against a particular group and works a hardship in their case. I shall now consider section 41, and I would impress upon the committee that if this bill of mine is passed it does not mean that the old section 41 will be done away with; but the objectionable clauses which were introduced two years ago will be abandoned and section 41 will remain as it was before that time. Section 41, dealing with the undesirable classes, says, in part, that any person who:
-shall, by word or act, create or attempt to create riot or public disorder in Canada, or shall by common repute belong to or be suspected of belonging to any secret society or organization which extorts money from or in any way attempts to control any resident of Canada. ... or who is a member of or affiliated with any organization entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government; such person, for the purposes of this act, shall be considered as belonging to the prohibited or undesirable classes and shall be liable to deportation.
There you have the same trouble entering in. The whole question as to whether or not a man is undesirable, or whether or not he belongs to organizations that

are supposed to teach doctrines that are not in harmony with the welfare of the country, is left to the Department of Immigration to decide. I would suggest that we should be in keeping with the very best British practice if we condemned men only when they committed some overt act and not for merely thinking this or the other thing. In Japan, I believe, there is now a law against dangerous thoughts, and we seem to be approaching very near to the autocratic imperialism of Japan when we undertake to decide whether or not a man harbours dangerous ideas. It has been taken for granted in British countries that a man may believe whatever he likes so long as he does not in any way interfere with his fellow-citizens or imperil the country. And that is sound ground to take. In section 16, I take exception particularly to the following:
Any person suspected of an offence under this section may forthwith be arrested and detained without a warrant by any officer for examination and deportation.
That, it seems to me, is going further than we can imagine possible in any British statute. It is bad enough to arrest, without warrant, any man who is really guilty, but in this case even if a man is only suspected of doing something he may be summarily arrested without warrant, and without trial deported, though he might happen to be a British subject. That is an intolerable situation. Section 17, which is amended in harmony with the other, provides:
Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen or a person having Canadian domicilehas done so and so. That is where it touches the British-born. If a man is foreign-born I presume he may have some sort of protection at the hands of a foreign consul; but if a man is British-born he has no domicile, and has not even a chance for naturalization. That comes in in another act. Provision is made in the Naturalization Act that a man, even if naturalized, may be de-naturalized at will. I have not introduced any bill with regard to that act, but, as amended in 1919, it fits into this nicely. Most of us had not realized that in order for a Britisher to obtain rights before the courts in this country, he had to be naturalized. But that is the case. It will be seen, therefore, that this catches a man in any case if he is considered undesirable. The British-born man has no domicile, and if he is naturalized he may be de-naturalized. Then

Immigration Act
we come further to the amendment to the amendment. It was considered, a few days after this amendment to the Immigration Act had been passed, that it was not strong enough and did not quite meet the needs of the time, and so still more stringent regulations were introduced. Section 41, as again amended, contains an extra clause with regard to undesirables:
Any one who without lawful authority assumes any powers of government In Canada or in any part thereof-
-may he declared an undesirable. That is to say, any man belonging to an organization that undertakes a certain kind of work which may be considered by somebody as work that ought to be done by the Government, may be declared an undesirable and without any impartial authority to try the case he may be summarily deported. Further on there is this clause:
Provided that this section shall not apply to any person who is a British subject either by reason of birth In Canada or by reason of naturalization in Canada.
There is where the difficulty comes in again with regard to naturalization. Most of our English immigrants coming to this country took it for granted that they had certain rights in the country and would receive full protection from the law. They did not consider it necessary to become naturalized, and this clause therefore places them in a far more difficult and helpless position than in the case with persons born in Germany, Austria, or Russia.
Do I understand from my hon. friend that a man born in Scotland and coming out here has to become naturalized?

Yes, before he
can obtain protection from this act; otherwise he is liable to deportation.

I think the hon. member
is quite wrong. If a man was born in Scotland he is a British subject and does not require to be naturalized at all.

Yes, otherwise
he may be deported.
Yes, back to Scotland.

That is my point; he has no chance. This proviso relates to any person who is a British subject either by reason of birth in Canada or by reason of naturalization in this country. But since a Scotsman is a subject of Canada
neither by birth in Canada nor by reason of naturalization here, he may be deported under the provisions of this act.
That is to say, his British citizenship by reason of birth in Scotland will not avail him in Canada under this act.

That is it. Subsection 2 says:
* Proof that any person who belongs to or was within the description of any of the prohibited or undesirable classes within the meaning of this section at any time since the fourth day of May, 1910, shall for all purposes of this act be deemed to establish prima facie that he still belongs to such prohibited or undesirable class or classes.
We have here introduced a retroactive clause-if it can ibe shown that prior to the 4th May, 1910, a person belonged to any of these undesirable classes, it should be at least prima facie evidence that he still belongs to them. I am no lawyer, but I have always thought that one of the fundamental principles of British law was that a man is to be considered innocent until he is proven guilty. Here it is provided that if he belongs to a certain class prima facie he is guilty. He is required to establish his own innocence of the "crime"-in this case of whether or not he belongs to any of these undesirable classes to which he belonged some years previously.
I do not think it is necessary at this time for me to say anything further with regard to the unfair and anti-British character of this legislation. I have perhaps emphasized the fact that it applies to Britishers. I should like to go a little bit further than that, because I think I have enough of the spirit of the Britisher in my own being to believe that everyone ought to have a fair chance in this country. I do not think the British-born want any greater privileges than any other body; I do not think that any of us who happen to be Canadian-born want any special privileges; and the idea in introducing this legislation is that we should give a fair chance to every man, Canadianjborn and1 non-Canadian born, and that if he is doing anything in any sehse detrimental to the best interests of the community he shall be regularly tried in open court, and if found guilty, deported, if you will-but given a fair trial first.
That, Mr. Chairman, as briefly as I can put it, is the contention embodied in this bill. I do not see how we could get at these subsections without having gone
Immigration Act

into that general question. I would read the first clause again:
1. iSubsection one of section two of chapter twenty-five of the statutes of 1919, being "An Act to amend The Immigration Act," is amended by repealing all such subsection from the proviso in subparagraph (t) to the end of the said subsection.
Section agreed' to.

I am heartily in sympathy with this measure and for the information of the hon. member (Mr. Woods-worth) who has just resumed his seat I might say that, with the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and several other hon. members, I opposed the law which it is now sought to repeal when it was first placed upon the statute books two years ago, at a time when this House seemed to be suffering from "jumpiness" and "nerves" induced by the long war. We had the idea that we could handle this question of undesirable immigrants very much better by permitting the immigration authorities, rather than our courts of justice, to pass upon their cases. I saw nothing at that time, nor have I seen anything since, which would cause me to alter my opinion that the proper forum for dealing with these cases is the court of justice in the district where the suspected party may be found.
I have some hesitation, Mr. Chairman, in speaking of immigration measures, for the reason that I happen to be the only member of a certain race in this House, and when I support a measure of this kind a portion of the press declare the following day that the measure is wanted only by a certain class of undesirable Jews whose views are put forward in the House by the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs.) So I fear I am rendering a disservice to the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr Woodsworth) by backing up his measure; my support may do him more harm than good. I have been suffering for some time from attacks of this kind from certain elements in the community, particularly in the city of Montreal.
Now, I should like to cite to the committee something which appeared in the Star of Montreal yesterday, which I think will convey to them some idea of how foreign immigrants are looked upon in certain quarters. The article is entitled:
Civic Body to discuss influx of foreigners with resultant crime
Sixty per cent of serious crimes here committed by Foreigners, Official Declares-Would restrict flow into country.

Then the article proceeds:
The flow of foreigners into Canada, with a consequent increase in the number of serious crimes, will be discussed by a special committee of the City Council this afternoon. Aid. Trepanier will preside.
The name "Trepanier" is rather signi-fieant; it suggests the necessity of the operation of trepanning.
Correspondence will be read from the Union of Canadian Municipalities and from the Merchants' Association of Montreal, dealing with the subject, and pointing out the danger of an unrestricted flow of foreigners into the bigger cities.
A letter from J. Fitzgerald, manager of the Merchants' Association, states it is entirely too easy for criminal characters to come into Canada, and entirely too difficult to have them removed after they get into the country.
"I believe that eighty per cent-
This is what Mr. Fitzgerald believes:
I believe that eighty per cent of the serious crimes in Montreal are committed by people who have come into the city only a few months previous to the commission of the crime," says Mr. Fitzgerald.
I suppose he wishes to imply that as they remain longer in the country their desire to commit crimes becomes less,-that they are filled with a desire to commit crimes only for the first few months after they arrive. The article continues:
"The police, when they discover that bad characters are here, seem to have every difficulty in having them sent out of the country."
Then there is this significant paragraph:
The secretary-treasurer of the Union of Canadian Municipalities, A. D. Shibley, of Montreal,-
Whoever he is; I never heard of him.
-writing to Aid. Trepanier-
You will notice, correspondence is going on between Trepanier and Shibley which is designed to affect public opinion in the district.
A. D. Shibley, of Montreal, writing to Aid. Trepanier to offer co-operation in the movement to restrict foreign immigration, declared that from police head-quarters he had found that last year sixty per cent of the serious crimes, such as murder and robbery with violence, were committed by foreigners, whereas, in proportion to their numbers, fifteen per cent should be their percentage.
He allows them the right to commit crime, but only to the extent of fifteen per cent.
There was also a financial loss by burning of buildings and stocks of merchandise which it was known was attributable to foreigners, but in most cases it was impossible to prove it, and this cost the city millions every year.

Immigration Act
That is the kind of propaganda which is being indulged in by certain elements in the community.
A bill similar to this was introduced on two occasions by hon. members in this House in the last Parliament. The first bill, I believe, was sponsored by Hon. Mr. Calder, at that time Minister of Immigration and Colonization. After the war was over the government of which he was a member felt that there was no further necessity for any such drastic legislation. Mr. Calder's bill took away from the Department of Immigration the right to decide questions as to the desirability or undesirability of certain immigrants. The bill passed this House without opposition, but when it went to the Senate it met an untimely end. Later a bill of the same nature was introduced by the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), but it also met the same fate when it reached the Senate. So I want to warn my good friend from Winnipeg that the passage of this bill may be met by some opposition when it reaches-I was going to say, that irresponsible Chamber, but I do not know that I will

that Chamber which is not responsible to the people. I assure him that if his bill passes this House and is defeated in the other Chamber I will support him from year to year until it becomes law, because I think it is a step in the right direction. It is something which is in consonance with British tradition and British practice, and it should pass this Chamber, unanimously.

Mr. Chairman, I think the suggestion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was the correct one in regard to the measure now before the committee, and I was glad to note that the promoter of the bill (Mr. Woodsworth) was willing to adopt that suggestion. This bill is a short one, but it involves a study of thirty or forty intricate sections and subsections of three or four distinct Acts of Parliament, and it would be idle for a committee of this size, with the time at our disposal, to give proper consideration to the important questions raised by the bill. I did not know the matter was coming on this afternoon, but I have hastily glanced over the various enactments-
I would like to ask the hon. member how long it took his government to pass this act in the first place? He suggests that the matter involves a good deal of investigation.

In the first place, the matter received long consideration before it reached the House, and it was considered at great length in the House during the session in which it was passed. In my opinion there are not more than four or five members of the committee who understand this proposal, and I think I would be in the majority, of those who do not. I doubt if any one but the promoter himself does understand it. If such a measure as this is to be placed on our statute book, by all means let us understand it; let us have proper consideration of the various clauses. The suggestion of the Prime Minister was that the matter should go to a small committee to be fully considered in all its aspects and reported to this House. The Committee of the Whole can never fully examine the various clauses that are affected. My hon. friend who last spoke (Mr. Jacobs), in his own jocular way, endeavoured, I think, rather to minimize the importance of the question of the class of immigration that should be permitted to come into Canada. But it is a very large and very important question for this Dominion and one which should not be lightly dealt with. It is just possible that the present law is in some respects too drastic. I, for one, realize that it was placed on the statute book at a critical time in the history of the country. That critical period has more or less passed away, and it is quite possible that the law should be modified. But I have not in the time at my disposal been able to grasp fully the meaning or import of the proposal, nor have I been able to come to any conclusion as to what other legislation will be affected if the bill is passed and put into operation. For that reason, I think the promoter of the bill would do well to suggest that the committee rise and report progress, on the understanding that the bill be referred to a special committee with power to inquire into the matter and report fully to the House at the earliest possible moment.

I look
upon this question as a judicial one. I am familiar with the conditions existing in Montreal, and I know that no part of the country has received more foreigners during the last ten years or so than that city. We are all interested in protecting the standing of Canada and seeing that justice is meted out to members of all classes and all creeds coming into this country. But, like the member for South Wellington (Mr. Immigration Act

Guthrie), I am unable to give an intelligent decision on the action taken by the member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), and I would strongly support the idea of having the matter referred to a small committee of competent men so that the matter can be examined and inquired into. During the last few years the charge has been repeatedly made in the press of Montreal -I do not know whether or not it is well founded-that a large number of the crimes committed in the city have been committed by recent arrivals in this country. It is a case of protection of the people, not only of Montreal, hut of the whole of Canada, and the Government would be well advised to give this matter mature consideration through a small committee of competent men. I Support that idea and hope the Government will give effect to it.
All that has been asked, as I understand it, toy this toil is that the law toe made the same as it was previous to 1919.
Nobody here knows what that was.

I find myself in much the same position as the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). In attempting hastily to get the full import of this bill that is before the committee I found it necessary to examine many sections of the amended Immigration Act, and it is quite impossible, in the short time at one's disposal, to get an intelligent view of the whole matter. When the 'bill was before the House on a former occasion-I think on its second reading-the suggestion was made that it would toe referred to a special committee. I was certainly under the impression that that procedure was to toe followed, and I cannnot understand at the moment, having Come into the chamber after the consideration of the bill was commenced, how it has reached its present Stage. To my mind, the measure should be referred to a committee, and* it should be done at once. I am free to say that I am in general accord with the principle of the bill. The amendments to the act, particularly those drastic amendments which were passed in 1919 giving power to the officials of the Department of Immigration, to deport people without any fair trial, are not in accord with British practice and should not remain on our statute book. The question, however, is a large one. The bill seeks to repeal a good many sections of the act, and11 think it could well toe re-

ferred to a special committee for report. I would offer the further observation that the committee should be appointed at the earliest possible day and should make its report to the House as soon as it can, so that we may consider the matter and deal with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am glad that apparently we have reached unanimity on this matter. It is quite true, as my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) has said, that when the bill was before the House on a former occasion I indicated that from the point of view of the Government it should be referred to a special committee, and that the Government would take steps to ascertain the names of the members who should compose that committee. When the Whips undertook to get the names of the committee, I was informed that the leader of the Opposition objected to having the matter discussed by a special committee at all. I was unable to understand what objection there could be to that course because it seemed to me it would be impossible to have the bill satisfactorily dealt with in any other way, and I spoke to the leader of the Opposition personally about it, so as to make quite sure that that was his view. He expressed to me the opinion, quite emphatically, that he thought the bill ought to be threshed out here in Committee of the Whole instead of being referred to a special committee. As I said this afternoon, I did not like to proceed by way of special committee if there was any real objection to that course on the part of any group in the House. I think we have had sufficient discussion this afternoon to convince everyone that it would be impossible to have this bill properly dealt with in Committee on the Whole, and I therefore now move, Mr. Chairman, that the committee rise and report progress.

Motion agreed to.
Progress reported.

On the Order for the House to again go into committee on Bill No. 17, to amend the Criminal Code, Mr. Woodsworth:

speechtext:
As this bill is related, I think, in some particulars to the

Immigration Act
one we have just referred to a special committee, I think it would be better to have it referred to the same committee. I therefore move that Bill No. 17 be referred to the committee to which Bill No. 16 was referred, and that this Order be discharged.
That procedure is quite satisfactory to me. I think it is much preferable that the matter should be threshed out in a special committee.

There is just this distinction between the present bill to amend the Criminal Code, and the one with which the House has just dealt. The present proposal is a very simple one, dealing practically with a single subject of the Criminal Code and involving the amendment of only one act of Parliament and one or two sections of that act. It relates to the crime known to our law under the name of sedition also to criminal conspiracies, I think. That is a matter, I think, that might fairly be dealt with by the Committee of the Whole House. However, I am not opposed to sending the bill to a special committee. I was unaware that my leader had taken a position in regard to this matter. I had never consulted him about it, but I am satisfied that if he had been here this afternoon and had heard the discussion so far as it has proceeded, he would have come to the conclusion that a special committee was proper in that instance. In the present case, speaking for myself, I am not opposed to this bill going to a special committee, although it contains a much simpler proposal than that involved in the amendment to the Immigration Act.

On motion of Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) Bill No. 45, to amend the Bankruptcy Act, was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On section 1-1919, c. 36, s. 3 amended:
Explain.

I may say that a bill similar to this was introduced last year by me, but it failed to receive the support of the Government, which makes it necessary for me to trouble this Parliament with a like measure. This bill provides that it shall be an added ground for the making of a petition in bankruptcy if the debtor gives notice to any of his creditors that he has suspended or is about to suspend payment of any of his debts, and secondly, if he ceases to meet his liabilities generally as they become due.
Inasmuch as this bill deals with a somewhat technical matter known practically to the legal profession only, I would suggest that it be referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee for further study, so that we might have an opportunity of hearing from various delegations and others who are interested in the measure.

I move that the committee rise and report progress.

speechtext: I move that Bill 45 be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce.

Just for the purpose of making myself clear on the point of order, Mr. Speaker, is it in order after a bill has been committed to the Committee of the Whole House to take it from that committee and send it to a select standing committee? If it is desired to refer a bill to a select standing committee, should not the motion be made immediately after the second reading, and before the bill has been referred to the Committee of the Whole House? I am raising the point of order simply that I may be enlightened.

A case of this kind does not often happen, but Bourinot provides a precedent for it. At page 527, fifth edition of Bourinot I find the following:
In case the committee of the whole has reported progress-*
As in this case.
-a motion may be made immediately before fixing the committee for a future date that the bill be referred to a select standing or other committee.
This is a case in point.

The House resumed from May 1, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Church.
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government of Canada should give early and favourable consideration to the report of the International Joint Commission on the St. Lawrence River Waterway, and request the Government of the United States to join with Canada in making an international agreement for carrying out the work so recommended.

When the debate on this matter
was adjourned a few days ago, I was thinking that we would have to be careful in dealing with this project in Canada. When the people on the other side of the line come forward with a project of this nature they generally have a motive of interest. In fact everybody in this life acts from a motive of interest, and when I see the people living in the districts of the Great Lakes advocating this enterprise and many members endorsing it I am but little surprised.
Within the last few weeks we have seen in the newspapers that representatives of the United States' Senate favour this measure. Senator King, from Utah, and Mr. Ten Eyck, Member of Congress, for Buffalo have said:	We may have a piece

of land down the St. Lawrence valley, and we may buy another piece of land along the Great Lakes, to carry on our international project in Canada, but when the scheme is supported by these people who are interested so much it seems to me perhaps it is not a beneficial thing for our country.
The United States is surely the country which will derive the most benefit from this enterprise. Of course on our side certain districts of this country will benefit if the project is carried on, from the construction, but they will especially benefit from the development of that waterway. It will certainly he a great benefit to all the harbours and wharves situated along the Great Lakes, and will be a benefit to the ports of Detroit, Port Huron and Chicago, and even of Fort William. Steamers will carry in their holds gold and merchandise.
The people on the other side of the line who propose this project are entitled to do so. They have a right to advocate the policy best calculated to satisfy their ambitions, but I am convinced that the measure will be against the interests of Canada as a whole. For the past two months an educational campaign has been carried on in favour of the project. The United States, in order to obtain an advantage in the matter of transportation, have had the International Joint Commission report printed and distributed. The United States Senate passed a measure adopting that report and they sent it to Canada to try to obtain the approval of the representatives of this country in the House of Commons.
Is it advisable for a country like ours, which can develop itself within its own boundaries, to endeavour to associate with the people of the United States, to give them the advantage of knowing everything about our system of navigation, of importation, about all the secrets of the St. Lawrence river, its weak points, if there are any, and many other matters which affect the safety of our country and which should be kept secret. If we open our country to their steamships, within twenty-five years Canada will be their own because if a joint board is appointed that will have control of this new channel, we may be quite sure that influences of all kinds will be brought to bear upon that board to our disadvantage.
In my opinion-and my hon. friends opposite are not obliged to make the confession-this project will be very advantageous to them and perhaps to them only in the present situation and for perhaps

St. Lawrence Waterway
twenty-five years to come. But when they consider their prosperity, they should not be too ambitious. The province of Ontario at the present time is a rich province; it is getting along well and making all the progress it may desire. It is one of the oldest provinces of Confederation and it has surely attained the aims which it has had since Confederation.
Will the hon. gentleman deny us seaports?

I do not wish to deny Ontario seaports, but the ports which it has now are developing well and in the near future it may have the advantage of all the other ports that may exist in Canada. But if the people of that province want for themselves a channel that will bring to them the fullest measure of prosperity at the expense of the maritime provinces and the western provinces, I think they want a little too much under the circumstances, especially when such a project would mean burdening the whole people of Canada with an expenditure of nearly $300,000,000. This project cannot be seriously considered under present conditions because our finances are not in such a state as to warrant the investment of such a large amount of money in bringing such an enormous scheme to a successful conclusion. On account of the need for economy in public expenditure, many public works throughout the country have been stopped. Many provinces require some money for drydocks and public services. The Esqui-malt drydock is still unfinished and a large amount of money is needed to complete it. In different parts of Canada, there are wharves that are in need of repair, and there are channels to be dug so that they may be deep enough for the steamers that have to pass through them.
If we want to develop our country by providing further water transportation facilities, there is the Georgian Bay canal, which has been mooted for many years back. It would be a useful development for Canada, and it would shorten the route by 300 miles, if it is given preference to the St. Lawrence waterway. By the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, the people not only of Ontario, but of the whole of Canada, will benefit; and in northern Ontario better progress will be made, because the settlers of to-day and of tomorrow will have better transportation facilities in that district than, exist at present.
On looking at the report, which has been laid on the Table of this House, and copies of which have been sent to every member by direction of the Prime Minister, I see that many questions were asked, but the answers that have been given to those questions should have been given more plainly, because, upon those answers, depends the question whether the project of the St. Lawrence waterway is a good thing or not as regards Canada. The question is not so much whether it is right to spend a great deal of money on a project, as whether, when you invest money, under our present financial conditions, good results will he obtained. At pages 183 and 184 of the report, it may be seen that the answers, which were given to the questions put before the commission so as to inform the two governments of the United States and Canada, are not very clear. Question 6, which, to my mind, is a vital question as regards Canada's interests, reads:
What method of control is recommended for the operation of the improved waterway to secure its most beneficial use?
The answer read's:
The commission recommends (a) that such navigation works as do not lie wholly within one country or are not capable of economic and efficient operation withni one country as complete and independent units, be operated under the direction of the International Board as set forth in recommendation No. 7: (b) that all navigation works other than those particularly mentioned in (a) be operated by the country in which they are located with the right of inspection by the International Board as set forth in recommendation No. 8; (c) that power works' be operated by the country in which they are located as set forth in recommendation No. 9.
The "power works" are indeed, Mr. Speaker, the corner stone of the whole St. Lawrence waterways Scheme. No specific method of control is mentioned. That answer is an example of the answers given in the report. We have rio definite answers to any of the most important questions concerning this project. There are no facts available, and what little information we have been given is as vague as the passing clouds. Let me read question No. *9 and the an'swer thereto:
WThat traffic, both incoming and outgoing, in kind and quantity, is likely to be carried upon the proposed route both at its inception and in the future, consideration to be given not only to present conditions, but to probable changes therein resulting from the development of industrial activities due to availability of large quantities of hydraulic power?
Answer. To this question also it is impossible to give a specific answer, in the absence of definite information as to all the factors that will enter into the problem.
St. Lawrence Waterway

I agree with that statement, because the commissioners [DOT] cannot possibly foretell what is likely to happen in the future. The answer continued:
The commission has brought together authoritative information as to the existing traffic between the tributary area and overseas points as well as between the same area and coastwise points on this continent, and has reached the general conclusion that sufficient traffic will seek the new water route, etc.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a " general conclusion " is hardly a substantial enough basis to act upon in an undertaking of such tremendous importance as this, and I am not surprised that the commission cannot say definitely what amount' of traffic there would be. Before embarking upon an enterprise involving, as this work certainly would, an enormous expenditure of money and is, in my humble opinion, a national risk, there should be submitted to the governments, both of the United States and of Canada, something more definite and concrete than the generalities that have been put forward. There should be absolutely reliable information on Which dependable calculations can be made. Indisputable authority based on the carefully considered findings of civil engineering experts should be available. In 1918 the St. Lawrence Power Company, an American corporation, constructed a dam at Massena in the state of New York and the undertaking was opposed by the government of our country. The work was carried out, nevertheless, because the International Joint Commission considered that it was necessary as a war measure; and this House may rest assured that the St. Lawrence will stand to lose a considerable degree of power by the construction of that dam, to the advantage of our neighbours.
As I said the other night, let us be content to develop what resources Providence has given to each province, and let us work together for the welfare of the country as a whole, each province being satisfied with its own and not interfering with others. We have the resources in Canada and it only remains for us to develop them for us to become a prosperous nation. But, I repeat, do not let us try to grab from one another what is not ours. In 1911 Sir Wilfrid Laurier was questioned regarding the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. He said that the work was one of national character and would be carried through for the benefit and welfare of the whole Dominion. He said, " If I could do it to-morrow, I would carry
out that work." And Mr. Pugsley, who was then Minister of Public Works, brought down an estimate of $3,000,000 to start survey work in connection with the Georgian Bay canal. This project was generally supported at that time, and members representing Ontario and the city of Toronto urged the government to carry it through. To-day, however, they have evidently abandoned that scheme and want another one which would involve the country in untold debt, without any definite assurance of success. I think that the Government would do well to consider this matter very seriously indeed before taking any action at all.
